Choices.A: Accept — the order adds $18,000 of operating income (3,000 × $8 − $6,000)
Choices.B: Accept — the order adds $24,000 of operating income
Choices.C: Reject — the added supervision is committed fixed cost and cannot change
Choices.D: Reject — the $30 price falls below the $40 normal selling price

CommonTrapReference: Treating a step fixed cost as permanently committed when the order crosses its threshold.
ExplanationCorrect: The order contributes 3,000 × ($30 − $22) = $24,000, but filling it pushes volume past a step threshold requiring $6,000 of additional supervision — a REAL incremental cost because it would not exist without the order. Net effect = $24,000 − $6,000 = +$18,000: accept. Step costs are fixed between jumps but variable across them, so relevance depends entirely on which side of the step the decision lands.
ExplanationWrongB: $24,000 counts the contribution but drops the supervision step. Because the order pushes volume past the threshold, that $6,000 exists only if Hartwell accepts — future and incremental by definition. Omitting it overstates the gain by exactly one-third of the claimed benefit.
ExplanationWrongC: Supervision here is not committed: it would never be hired but for this order, which is the definition of avoidable. Confusing cost BEHAVIOR inside a range with immutability ACROSS decisions rejects profitable business over an accounting label.
ExplanationWrongD: List price governs regular-channel economics, not special-order acceptance. With idle capacity and incremental costs fully covered plus $18,000 to spare, the discount to list is the mechanism of the gain, not evidence against it.
Stem: Hartwell Textiles receives a 3,000-unit special order at $30 per unit; variable cost is $22 per unit. Filling it pushes monthly volume past a step threshold requiring $6,000 of additional supervision that would not otherwise be needed. What is the correct decision?
Topic: C.141 Special order crossing a step fixed cost

Choices.A: 20,000 units — volume holds because contribution margin is unchanged
Choices.B: 22,728 units — ($200,000 + $300,000) ÷ $22, rounding up to cover the target fully

CommonTrapReference: Forgetting to recompute contribution margin after a variable-cost shock.
ExplanationCorrect: Required units = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM per unit = ($200,000 + $300,000) ÷ ($25 − $3) = $500,000 ÷ $22 = 22,727.3 → round UP to 22,728 units, because fractional units earn no fractional profit. The shock cut CM from $25 to $22, so holding $300,000 of operating income demands about 13.6% more volume — quantifying precisely why input inflation forces pricing or efficiency responses.
ExplanationWrongA: 20,000 units sufficed under the OLD $25 margin; at $22 those same units deliver only $440,000 against $500,000 required — a $60,000 shortfall. Volume must rise when unit margin falls.
ExplanationWrongC: $250,000 of fixed cost appears nowhere in the facts — inserting it inflates the numerator and the answer. Only actual fixed costs ($200,000) plus the grossed-up target ($300,000) belong in the formula.
ExplanationWrongD: Dividing the profit target alone by CM omits the $200,000 of fixed costs that must ALSO be covered before any profit exists. The resulting 13,636 units leave Riverton short of breakeven, let alone target.
Stem: Riverton Foods has fixed costs of $200,000 and currently sells 20,000 units at a $25 contribution margin, earning $300,000 of operating income. A $3 variable-cost increase cuts the margin to $22. How many units must Riverton sell to keep operating income at $300,000?
Topic: C.142 Cost-shock volume to hold target profit

Choices.A: Drop Customer Y — its allocated share of corporate overhead makes it unprofitable
Choices.B: Drop both customers and redeploy the account teams to prospecting
Choices.C: KEEP BOTH — Customer X nets +$50,000 and Customer Y nets +$30,000 before unavoidable allocations; dropping either surrenders real contribution while the overhead remains
Choices.D: Raise Customer Y's prices by at least 14% to force coverage of allocated corporate costs

CommonTrapReference: Letting allocated corporate overhead drive customer-level decisions.
ExplanationCorrect: Customer X: $200,000 − $120,000 variable − $30,000 dedicated service = +$50,000. Customer Y: $180,000 − $130,000 − $20,000 = +$30,000. The corporate allocation is UNAVOIDABLE — it persists whichever customers stay — so decision-relevant profitability is measured BEFORE it. Both accounts contribute real dollars; the allocation merely disguises Y's positive economics behind an arbitrary share.
ExplanationWrongA: The allocation made Y LOOK like a loss, but losing Y removes $30,000 of genuine contribution while the overhead keeps running in full. Decisions must compare contribution lost against costs ACTUALLY avoided.
ExplanationWrongB: Dropping X as well destroys $50,000 of contribution on top of Y's $30,000 while saving nothing either departure caused. Redeployment assumes instant replacement revenue prospects rarely deliver on schedule.
ExplanationWrongD: Pricing should track value and elasticity, not arbitrary allocations. Forcing a 14% increase to cover overhead that exists independently risks losing a positive contributor over a bookkeeping artifact — and if Y leaves anyway, the allocation simply redistributes onto X.
Stem: Controller Dana Walsh reviews two accounts: Customer X - revenue $200,000, variable costs $120,000, dedicated service $30,000; Customer Y - revenue $180,000, variable costs $130,000, dedicated service $20,000. Corporate overhead allocates $25,000 to each account. What decision does relevant analysis support?
FormulaReference: Customer net = revenue - VC - dedicated costs

Choices.A: Reject — the shift premium exceeds base labor rates and always erodes margin
Choices.B: Elevate — the move adds $20,000 of throughput contribution
Choices.C: Reject — constraint expansion never pays back within a year
Choices.D: ELEVATE — freed throughput of 400 hours × $50 = $20,000 exceeds the $12,000 premium, adding $8,000 of expected benefit

CommonTrapReference: Comparing the premium against base labor rates instead of against the throughput gained.
ExplanationCorrect: TOC values constraint-hours by what flows through them: each new hour yields $50 of contribution, so 400 hours are worth $20,000 regardless of what base labor is paid. Against the $12,000 premium, elevating nets +$8,000. The comparison is marginal benefit versus marginal cost OF THE CONSTRAINT — payroll benchmarking answers a different question entirely.
ExplanationWrongA: The premium-versus-base-rate comparison is beside the point: the second shift is not hired to be cheap, it is hired to unlock hours worth $50 each. What matters is whether unlocked throughput exceeds the unlocking cost — here $20,000 versus $12,000.
ExplanationWrongB: $20,000 counts only the throughput gained and ignores the $12,000 premium entirely. The decision is NET: +$8,000 after cost — direction right, number wrong.
ExplanationWrongC: 'Never pays back' is asserted, not computed. By construction this investment repays inside twelve months — $12K against $20K of annual benefit — and constraint capacity typically delivers that benefit every year thereafter.
Stem: Barlow Products' bottleneck earns $50 of contribution per hour. Operations proposes a second shift adding 400 constraint-hours per month at a $12,000 monthly premium. Should the second shift be added?
Topic: C.144 Elevating the constraint - second-shift economics
FormulaReference: TOC net = hours gained x CM/hour - premium

Choices.A: The reported drop in fixed cost per unit is a genuine saving that justifies accepting any reasonable order
Choices.B: Spreading fixed costs over more units LOWERS reported unit cost but saves nothing — total fixed dollars are unchanged, so decisions rest on incremental revenues and costs, not on unitized averages
Choices.C: Lower fixed cost per unit increases the breakeven point
Choices.D: Unit fixed cost is the primary driver of special-order acceptance decisions

CommonTrapReference: Mistaking denominator effects in unitized fixed cost for economic savings.
ExplanationCorrect: $100,000 spread over 10,000 units reports $10 per unit; over 12,500 units, $8. The company still wrote the same $100,000 check — the 'saving' is arithmetic on a denominator. Special-order decisions compare incremental REVENUE against incremental COST, and unitized fixed cost appears on neither side of that ledger. Managers who celebrate the thinner unit cost have confused a ratio with a resource.
ExplanationWrongA: If falling unit averages justified orders, every order above a shrinking average would clear review — including ones priced below variable cost that burn cash on every unit. Incremental revenue versus incremental cost is the test; the average is scenery.
ExplanationWrongC: Breakeven moves with the CONTRIBUTION margin ratio and total fixed dollars — neither changes because a denominator grew. Higher volume at the same structure sits FURTHER above breakeven, not below it.
ExplanationWrongD: Unitized fixed cost is precisely what relevance rules OUT of special-order analysis: the decision turns on incremental revenue against incremental cost. Anchoring acceptance logic on an average invites business that destroys value per unit.
Stem: A production manager recommends accepting an order because fixed cost per unit drops from $10 to $8 at the higher volume. Which evaluation is correct?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: Unitized fixed cost = denominator arithmetic, no cash saving

Choices.A: Captive pricing requires selling every component at full cost to remain profitable
Choices.B: Captive product pricing sells the platform near or below cost and earns margins on proprietary consumables — viable only where switching costs and lock-in keep customers buying the attached products
Choices.C: Captive pricing is illegal under antitrust law in all commercial forms
Choices.D: Captive pricing works best when consumables are commodity items available from many suppliers

CommonTrapReference: Judging platform losses without modeling the attached-consumable annuity.
ExplanationCorrect: Razor-and-blade economics price the INSTALLATION — printer, handle, machine — at near-zero margin to maximize installed base, then harvest high-margin CONSUMABLES whose demand is captive to that platform. Two conditions carry the model: the attach product must be proprietary or effectively locked, and switching friction must hold customers in. Wherever refills commoditize or contracts allow open substitutes, below-cost platforms become pure losses rather than investments.
ExplanationWrongA: Pricing the platform at full cost shrinks the installed base — the very annuity captive economics depend on. The model profits precisely by NOT recovering full cost up front, recouping it through the attached stream instead.
ExplanationWrongC: Legality turns on conduct — tying arrangements that foreclose competition raise antitrust questions — but captive pricing as such pervades legitimate commerce from razors to game consoles to coffee systems.
ExplanationWrongD: Commodity refills BREAK captivity: customers refill wherever cheaper, converting the platform from an investment into a gift to refill vendors. Proprietary or contractually locked consumables are the load-bearing condition of the entire model.
Stem: At the printer-line strategy review, the marketing director asks when below-cost platform pricing makes sense. Which explanation is correct?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: Platform near/below cost; margin on proprietary captive consumables

Choices.A: Accept — the order adds $60,000 of operating income
Choices.B: Reject — $42 sits below the $50 domestic list price and dilutes brand equity irrecoverably
Choices.C: ACCEPT — the order adds $100,000: the export house carries selling duties, so the 6% domestic commission never applies, and idle capacity means no displacement
Choices.D: Reject — international freight makes any sub-list export order unprofitable

CommonTrapReference: Deducting the avoided domestic commission anyway, or rejecting below-list orders on principle.
ExplanationCorrect: Relevant cost on this order is manufacturing only — $32 — because the export arrangement eliminates the domestic 6% selling commission AND the buyer bears freight AND idle capacity absorbs the volume. Incremental income = 10,000 × ($42 − $32) = +$100,000. The domestic list embeds a selling cost this channel simply does not incur, which is why cross-channel price gaps can reflect real cost differences rather than dilution.
ExplanationWrongA: $60,000 subtracts the commission the export house already absorbs — double-counting a cost this order does not incur. With no selling expense and no displacement, each unit carries the full $10 spread.
ExplanationWrongB: Brand-dilution claims require leakage into domestic channels at discount prices; the facts route resale through the export house in separate markets under its own pathway. No such leakage is asserted, so the argument has no factual footing here.
ExplanationWrongD: The exhibit states freight is borne by the buyer. Rejecting on costs another party pays substitutes assumption for arithmetic — and the arithmetic shows $100,000 of clean contribution.
Stem: Atlas Manufacturing's domestic price is $50 (variable manufacturing cost $32 plus a 6% selling commission). An export house offers to buy 10,000 units at $42 with buyer-paid freight; Atlas has idle capacity and pays no commission on these sales. Should the order be accepted?
Topic: C.147 Export order avoiding domestic selling commission

Choices.A: Two-part tariffs are inherently discriminatory and prohibited in ordinary commercial sales
Choices.B: The usage fee should recover full average total cost per unit
Choices.C: Entry fees should approach zero so customers face no barrier to adoption
Choices.D: A fixed access fee plus a usage charge near marginal cost lets the firm recover fixed costs through the entry fee while expanding usage among heterogeneous customers

CommonTrapReference: Confusing tariff structure with unlawful discrimination, or expecting usage fees to carry all fixed costs.
ExplanationCorrect: Two-part pricing separates the ACCESS decision from the USAGE decision: the entry fee harvests willingness-to-pay for membership (covering fixed costs and extracting surplus from heavy users), while usage priced near marginal cost keeps consumption efficient and broad. Clubs, warehouse memberships, software seats, and utility standing charges run on this architecture. Heterogeneous intensity is the feature: light users self-select via entry fees, heavy users generate usage margins.
ExplanationWrongA: Structure is not conduct: two-part schedules pervade lawful commerce. Antitrust scrutiny attaches to exclusionary designs, not to access-plus-usage pricing as such.
ExplanationWrongB: Loading average TOTAL cost into the usage fee taxes exactly the consumption the firm wants to grow and prices light users out. Moving fixed recovery into the entry fee is what makes near-marginal-cost usage viable.
ExplanationWrongC: Zero entry fees forfeit the mechanism itself: without an access charge, fixed costs must flow into usage pricing, which taxes consumption and prices out light users — the opposite of what barrier-free adoption promises.
Stem: The controller of a fitness-club chain explains why members pay an annual access fee PLUS low per-visit charges. Which statement about this two-part tariff is correct?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: Entry fee recovers fixed costs; usage priced near marginal cost
